draft.title: The first in, first out method
card: First in, first out (FIFO) is a way to cost inventory when the same item is bought at different prices. It assumes the oldest stock is sold first.
So when a sale is made, the cost of sales uses the earliest purchase prices still on hand. Cost of sales is the cost of the goods sold.
Example: a shop buys 10 units at $5, then 10 units at $6, and sells 12 units. Under FIFO the cost of sales is 10 × $5 + 2 × $6 = $62.
The units left on hand are the most recent purchases. Here, 8 units at $6 remain, so inventory on hand is valued at $48.
draft.remember: FIFO: sales take the oldest prices, and the stock left is at the newest prices.

a.q: Under FIFO, which cost is used first for the cost of sales?
opts: The price of the oldest stock on hand
The price of the most recent purchase
The average price of all stock on hand
The selling price of the goods sold
a.why: FIFO assumes the oldest stock is sold first, so cost of sales starts with the earliest purchase prices. Using the most recent purchase first is a different assumption, not FIFO.
a.clue: First in is the first to go out.

b.q: Priya's bike shop buys 5 helmets at $20, then 5 helmets at $24. It sells 7 helmets. Using FIFO, what is the cost of sales and the value of the helmets left?
opts: Cost of sales $148, helmets left $72
Cost of sales $164, helmets left $56
Cost of sales $148, helmets left $56
Cost of sales $164, helmets left $72
b.why: The 7 sold are the 5 at $20 and 2 at $24: $100 + $48 = $148. The 3 left are the newest, at $24 each, so $72. Taking the newest helmets first would give $164, which is not FIFO.
b.clue: Sell all the $20 helmets first, then take the rest from the $24 lot.

a.best: The price of the oldest stock on hand

problems.detail: The why says taking the newest helmets first would give $164. That is wrong: 5 × $24 + 2 × $20 = $160, with 3 × $20 = $60 left. The $164 and $56 distractors do not match the LIFO-style mistake the why describes, so the explanation teaches a false figure.
